Seminar Title:

Aerosol Variability and Its Climate Impacts over South Asia under Present and Future Anthropogenic Aerosol Emission Scenarios

Seminar Type:

Registration Seminar

Department:

Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Speaker Name:

Anushri Pal ( Rollno : 524er1010)

Speaker Type:

Venue:

Room No. 303, Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Date and Time:

12 Aug 2026 11:00

Contact:

Sushant Das

Abstract:

The climatic effects of aerosols in South Asia remain highly uncertain because of the complex contributions of natural and anthropogenic aerosols and their interactions with regional climate processes. This study examines the variability of total, dust, non-dust, and anthropogenic aerosols over South Asia using 7 CMIP6 models for the period 1995-2014. Model performance is evaluated against multiple datasets, including MERRA-2, MODIS, CRU, and AERONET. Taylor diagram and pattern-correlation analyses against MERRA-2 demonstrate that the CMIP6 multi-model mean (MMM) reproduces the observed AOD distribution with high fidelity during the pre-monsoon (MAM r = 0.895) and the summer monsoon season (JJAS r = 0.931). Among the models, MPI-ESM1-2-HAM exhibits the highest spatial skill during MAM (r = 0.931), and GFDL-ESM4 performs best during JJAS (r = 0.939). Dust aerosols peak during MAM and JJAS, whereas anthropogenic aerosols dominate throughout the year and account for the largest fraction of non-dust AOD. Comparisons between historical and hist-piAer simulations reveal that anthropogenic aerosol forcing exerts a significant influence on the regional climate. Furthermore, historical simulations that included changes in aerosol emissions reproduced the observed long-term temperature and precipitation trends reasonably well. In the CMIP6 MMM, the aerosol-induced surface cooling is partially offset by enhanced sensible heat flux during MAM (&DeltaT = &minus1.415 ℃&nbsp&DeltaTSH = 1.037 ℃) and by latent heat flux during JJAS (&DeltaT = &minus0.918 ℃&nbsp&DeltaTLE = 1.310 ℃),&nbspwhile weakened monsoon circulation and reduced moisture transport contribute to precipitation deficit over the CTCZ region for JJAS. Overall, these findings highlight the critical roles of anthropogenic aerosols in modulating the seasonal climate variability across South Asia and the need to improve aerosol representation in climate models to reduce uncertainties in future climate projections.
